events.title: Bush carries Georgia
events.text: George W. Bush carried Georgia by almost twelve points over Al Gore.

events.title: A new state flag
events.text: Governor Roy Barnes replaced the 1956 flag, which had featured the Confederate battle emblem.

events.title: Perdue elected
events.text: Sonny Perdue beat Barnes, the first Republican elected governor of Georgia since 1868.

events.title: Senate changes hands
events.text: After four Democratic senators switched parties, Republicans took control of the state Senate.

events.title: Republican House
events.text: Republicans won the Georgia House, holding both chambers for the first time since Reconstruction.

events.title: Foster-care cause
events.text: Rick Jackson became involved in FaithBridge Foster Care, which he co-founded and chairs.

events.title: The margin narrows
events.text: John McCain carried Georgia by five points, down from George W. Bush's seventeen in 2004.

events.title: Council seat
events.text: Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to the Atlanta City Council from southwest Atlanta.

events.title: Deal elected
events.text: Nathan Deal beat Roy Barnes for governor, 53 to 43 percent.

events.title: Deal re-elected
events.text: Deal won a second term over Jason Carter, the grandson of Jimmy Carter.

events.title: Cobb votes Democratic
events.text: Hillary Clinton carried Cobb County, the first Democrat to do so since Jimmy Carter in 1976.

events.title: Gwinnett follows
events.text: Clinton also carried Gwinnett County, last won by a Democrat in 1976.

events.title: Mayor by 821 votes
events.text: Bottoms won the Atlanta mayoral runoff over Mary Norwood by 821 votes after a recount.

events.title: Cash bail ended
events.text: Mayor Bottoms signed an ordinance ending cash bail for most people held on city-ordinance charges.

events.title: Kemp elected
events.text: Brian Kemp beat Stacey Abrams, 50.2 to 48.8 percent, just above the majority that avoids a runoff.

events.title: Six-week abortion law
events.text: Governor Kemp signed House Bill 481, banning most abortions after about six weeks; it took effect in 2022.

events.title: Housing plan
events.text: Bottoms unveiled a plan for $1 billion to create or preserve 20,000 affordable homes by 2026.

events.title: “Go home”
events.text: On 29 May, during protests after the murder of George Floyd, Bottoms told people damaging property to go home.

events.title: Rayshard Brooks
events.text: On 12 June Atlanta police shot Rayshard Brooks at a Wendy's; the police chief resigned the next day.

events.title: Mask order lawsuit
events.text: Kemp sued Bottoms and the city council over Atlanta's order requiring face coverings.

events.title: Pandemic staffing
events.text: Jackson's companies began state contracts that reached about $1 billion by 2026, starting with a no-bid pandemic contract.

events.title: Biden by 11,779
events.text: Joe Biden carried Georgia by 11,779 votes, the first Democrat to win it since 1992.

events.title: Senate runoffs
events.text: On 5 January Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock won both Senate seats for the Democrats.

events.title: One term
events.text: On 6 May Bottoms announced that she would not seek a second term as mayor.

events.title: To the White House
events.text: Bottoms became a senior adviser to President Biden and director of public engagement.

events.title: Kemp re-elected
events.text: Kemp beat Abrams again, by 7.5 points.

events.title: Split tickets
events.text: On the same ballot Warnock won 132,444 more votes than Abrams, and later won his runoff.

events.title: Trump by 2.2
events.text: Donald Trump carried Georgia by 2.2 points over Kamala Harris.

events.title: The mountains
events.text: Towns and Union counties in the North Georgia mountains each gave Trump 81 percent.

events.title: The Black Belt
events.text: Hancock County, in Georgia's Black Belt, gave Harris 67.5 percent.

events.title: Jimmy Carter dies
events.text: Jimmy Carter, governor from 1971 to 1975 and president, died in Plains at the age of one hundred.

events.title: Bottoms runs
events.text: On 20 May Bottoms launched her campaign for governor.

events.title: Jackson runs
events.text: On 3 February Rick Jackson launched his campaign in Alpharetta, pledging $50 million of his own money.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 19 May Bottoms won the Democratic primary outright; Burt Jones led Jackson for the Republicans.

events.title: Jackson wins runoff
events.text: On 16 June Jackson beat Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones, 52.6 to 47.4 percent.

events.title: Former governors endorse
events.text: Kemp, Nathan Deal and Sonny Perdue endorsed Jackson on 18 June.

events.title: No Libertarian
events.text: The Libertarian Party failed to qualify for the statewide ballot.

events.title: Trump endorses Jackson
events.text: In late July President Trump endorsed Jackson in a post on Truth Social.

events.title: One debate
events.text: On 6 October Bottoms and Jackson met in their only joint debate, on Atlanta News First.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: In-person early voting runs from 13 to 30 October; more than a million ballots had been cast by 20 October.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Georgians choose between Jackson, Bottoms and seven write-in candidates.

chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; certified results). It is a simplification: Georgia elects its governor in its own race, and many Georgians split their tickets (in 2022 Brian Kemp won by 7.5 points on the same ballot on which Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, led the Senate race), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Georgia, so outer states are cut at the edge.
